en.homeWhoProfits: Who makes money from a dot?
en.homeWhoProfitsBody: A TLD can behave like national revenue, recurring infrastructure rent, a corporate asset, an auction prize or even a profitable withdrawal.
en.economicsCasesIntro: TLDs are naming infrastructure, but they can also create public revenue, recurring registry income, scarcity rents, acquisition value and financial barriers to entry. These cases keep unlike metrics separate rather than forcing them into one league table.
en.economicsSelectionNote: Selection rule: each case illustrates a distinct economic mechanism and is supported by attributable financial or institutional evidence. Revenue, valuation, auction price and public receipts are not interchangeable measures.
en.economicsModelsTitle: Eight ways money enters the namespace
en.economicsModelsSub: The same DNS root can generate very different economic relationships.
en.economicsCasesGridSub: Read each number in its own accounting context. The purpose is comparison of mechanisms, not a ranking of “most valuable TLDs”.
en.economicCaseDrawerSub: Documented financial evidence linked to this TLD. Different metric types are deliberately kept separate.
en.downloadEconomicCasesSub: CSV · economic mechanisms, strings and sources
en.downloadEconomicMetricsSub: CSV · values, currencies, accounting basis and sources
en.econModelSovereignRentBody: A country-code namespace becomes a material source of government revenue because global demand attaches value to its two-letter code.
en.econModelNationalContractBody: A state monetizes its ccTLD through a commercial registry or marketing agreement rather than operating a mass-market registrar business itself.
en.econModelOperatorAcquisitionBody: The company operating one or more namespaces is bought, turning expected registry cash flows into a transaction value.
en.econModelRecurringRegistryBody: Large installed bases and annual renewals can create highly recurring infrastructure revenue, but company-level results must not be mislabeled as revenue from one TLD.
en.econModelValuationRegulationBody: A registry contract can underpin billion-dollar valuation while price controls, public-interest duties and change-of-control review shape the asset.
en.econModelScarcityAuctionBody: When multiple applicants want the same string, scarcity can be converted into an auction price before the registry has sold a single domain.
en.econModelPrivateSettlementBody: Historical 2012-round mechanism: applicants could receive consideration for withdrawing from contention, so abandoning a string could generate accounting gains. Private contention resolution, including settlement agreements and compensation for withdrawal, is prohibited in the 2026 round.
en.econModelEntryBarrierBody: Application fees and additional evaluation costs determine who can afford to compete for a place in the root.
en.econAiQuestion: Can two letters become a national revenue asset?
en.econAiFact: Anguilla’s 2026 budget estimates EC$253.6 million from Domain Name Registration, up from EC$104.3 million actual in 2024.
en.econAiReading: The AI boom turned a legacy country code into something resembling a digital natural resource: global semantic demand generates public revenue for a small jurisdiction.
en.econTvQuestion: Can a country lease the commercial meaning of its country code?
en.econTvFact: Tuvalu’s 2024 budget allocated A$5.60 million to the Dot TV Marketing Agreement and projected A$5.87 million for 2026.
en.econTvReading: .tv shows a different sovereign model from .ai: value is captured through a commercial agreement tied to the global meaning of “TV”.
en.econIoQuestion: What is the operator of a fashionable ccTLD worth?
en.econIoFact: A secondary industry source reported that Afilias acquired Internet Computer Bureau, operator of .io, .ac and .sh, for US$70.17 million in cash in 2017.
en.econIoReading: The case shows that economic value can sit in the operating company and its registry cash flows, not in a simple notion that a TLD itself has a sale price.
en.econComQuestion: What does mature registry scale look like?
en.econComFact: Verisign reported US$1.66 billion of company revenue and US$1.12 billion of operating income in 2025; .com and .net ended the year with 173.5 million registrations combined.
en.econComReading: Recurring renewals, scale and high switching friction make mature registry infrastructure economically unlike a normal one-off domain sale. The figures are Verisign company results, not .com-only revenue.
en.econOrgQuestion: Can a registry contract underpin a billion-dollar valuation?
en.econOrgFact: The proposed 2019 acquisition of Public Interest Registry was publicly priced at US$1.135 billion, financed in part by a US$360 million term loan facility; ICANN ultimately withheld consent.
en.econOrgReading: .org exposes the tension between financial value and stewardship: an economically valuable recurring namespace can still be constrained by contractual approval, regulation and public-interest expectations.
en.econAuctionQuestion: How much will applicants pay for scarcity before launch?
en.econAuctionFact: ICANN last-resort auctions produced winning prices of US$135 million for .web, US$41.501 million for .shop and US$25.001 million for .app.
en.econAuctionReading: A string can acquire a nine-figure clearing price before operating revenue exists. The price reflects contention scarcity and strategic expectations, not an appraisal of the TLD as property.
en.econWithdrawalQuestion: Can losing or withdrawing be profitable?
en.econWithdrawalFact: Rightside reported a US$22.103 million net gain in 2014 and US$9.403 million in 2015 from withdrawals of interests in gTLD applications.
en.econWithdrawalReading: Private contention resolution created an unusual incentive: an application could have financial value even when the applicant never became registry operator.
en.econFeeQuestion: How expensive is the right to compete for the root?
en.econFeeFact: The base evaluation fee was US$185,000 in the 2012 round and is US$227,000 per application in the 2026 round, before certain additional fees or support discounts.
en.econFeeReading: The application fee is not a purchase price for a TLD. It is an entry cost into an uncertain evaluation process, and therefore part of the economic barrier to participation.
en.release0715: Economics of the Dot: economic cases, financial metrics, Explorer links and source-backed models added without conflating revenue, valuation, auctions or public receipts.
en.angle6: How country codes, renewals, auctions, acquisitions and application fees turn naming infrastructure into economic value.
en.homeWhoBelongsBody: Some TLDs express language, place, identity, community rules or social protection. A dot can be more than an address: it can become a claim of belonging.
en.socialCaseDrawerSub: Documented community rules and social purposes are shown as facts; the broader social meaning remains an editorial reading.
en.socialCasesTitle: The social life of the dot
en.socialCasesIntro: TLDs can mark language, territory, identity, professions, rights or community norms. These cases examine what a namespace asks of the people who use it and the community it claims to represent.
en.socialSelectionNote: This is a curated social reading, not a ranking of “social success”. Registration volume, community value and cultural significance are different things.
en.socialModelsTitle: Six ways a namespace becomes social
en.socialModelsSub: These categories describe different social functions and can overlap within the same TLD.
en.socialCasesGridSub: From linguistic communities to local nexus rules, safety policies and non-Latin scripts.
en.downloadSocialCasesSub: CSV · community, identity, inclusion and social-policy cases
en.socialModelLanguageBody: A namespace can give a language or cultural community a visible place in global naming.
en.socialModelCivicBody: A local nexus can turn a place name into a membership signal rather than generic branding.
en.socialModelIdentityBody: A string can become a flag for shared identity, values or representation.
en.socialModelInstitutionBody: Eligibility, verification and governance can bind a namespace to a defined community or institutional movement.
en.socialModelSafetyBody: Registry policies can try to create norms, protections or boundaries for vulnerable or sensitive communities.
en.socialModelScriptBody: Internationalized domain names remove the assumption that global naming must be written in Latin characters.
en.socialCatEligibility: Use Catalan online, promote Catalan culture, or address that community
en.socialCatGovernance: Community-based sponsored origin, now operated under an ICANN registry agreement
en.socialGalOrganization: PuntoGal is a non-profit organization rooted in Galician civil society
en.socialGalReinvestment: Profits are reinvested in promoting Galician language and culture
en.socialGalMemory: More than 7,000 .gal domains were collected for digital preservation in 2024
en.socialGayPurpose: A namespace explicitly framed around LGBTQ identity and a safer online space
en.socialGayDonation: The 2020 policies filed with ICANN committed 20% of registration revenue to recognized LGBTQ advocacy and activism charities
en.socialGayProtection: Additional measures targeted hate speech, cyberbullying and harassment
en.socialCoopEligibility: Restricted to cooperatives and eligible organizations supporting them
en.socialCoopVerification: Eligibility is verified and may be audited
en.socialNycNexus: Registrants must maintain a substantive lawful connection with New York City
en.socialNycConnection: The policy recognizes economic, cultural, historical, social or other lawful connections
en.socialKidsCommunity: A community application centered on children and child-related stakeholders
en.socialKidsProtection: The application framed .kids as a kids-friendly and kids-safe namespace
en.socialKidsDelegation: Delegated in 2022 to DotKids Foundation Limited
en.socialXxxSelfIdentification: The original sponsored model was based on voluntary self-identification by the adult-entertainment community
en.socialXxxPurpose: The charter included responsible practices, user choice and measures against illegal abusive material
en.socialXxxEvolution: The 2024 renewal moved from sponsorship to the Base Registry Agreement while carrying key commitments into PICs
en.socialIslamRepresentation: The applications sought to operate globally meaningful religious terms
en.socialIslamGovernment: GAC members and OIC states questioned community involvement, support and legitimacy
en.socialIdnScripts: Examples include Cyrillic, Arabic, Chinese and Devanagari top-level labels
en.socialIdnAccess: Users can navigate domain names in local languages and scripts instead of transliterating everything into Latin characters
en.socialIdnProcess: The IDN ccTLD Fast Track has enabled eligible countries and territories to request non-Latin country-name TLDs since 2009
en.socialCatQuestion: Can a TLD represent a language community rather than a state?
en.socialCatFact: The .cat charter says the namespace serves the Catalan Linguistic and Cultural Community. Eligibility includes using Catalan online, promoting Catalan culture or addressing that community.
en.socialCatReading: It separates cultural-linguistic belonging from state borders: a top-level domain can represent a community that is not reducible to one country.
en.socialGalQuestion: Can a namespace become part of a community’s cultural memory?
en.socialGalFact: PuntoGal is a non-profit organization that reinvests profits in Galician language and culture. In 2024, its official site reported that more than 7,000 .gal domains had been collected for preservation by national and regional libraries.
en.socialGalReading: The namespace functions not only as an identity marker but also as a corpus of digital life worth preserving.
en.socialGayQuestion: Can registry policy deliberately shape the social norms of a namespace?
en.socialGayFact: Policies filed with ICANN in 2020 committed 20% of registration revenue to recognized LGBTQ advocacy and activism charities and added measures against hate speech, cyberbullying and harassment.
en.socialGayReading: Here the registry is not neutral about social purpose: identity, redistribution and behavioral norms are built into the policy design.
en.socialCoopQuestion: What changes when a TLD verifies membership in a social and economic movement?
en.socialCoopFact: The .coop charter serves the international cooperative community. Current eligibility rules restrict registrations to cooperatives and qualifying support organizations and provide for verification.
en.socialCoopReading: The domain works as a membership signal: the string says something about the organizational model behind the registrant, not merely its website address.
en.socialNycQuestion: What does it mean to be “local” on a global network?
en.socialNycFact: The .nyc Nexus Policy requires registrants to maintain a substantive lawful connection with New York City and recognizes economic, cultural, historical, social and other lawful connections.
en.socialNycReading: The DNS becomes a boundary-making device: “New Yorker” is translated from a social idea into an eligibility rule.
en.socialKidsQuestion: Can a namespace make the Internet meaningfully safer for children?
en.socialKidsFact: DotKids Foundation applied for .kids as a community namespace centered on children and child-related stakeholders, framing it as kids-friendly and kids-safe. The TLD was delegated in 2022.
en.socialKidsReading: The case exposes the gap between labeling and protection: a trusted social meaning requires governance, enforcement and adoption, not merely a reassuring string.
en.socialXxxQuestion: Does putting sensitive content in a distinct namespace protect users, stigmatize a community, or both?
en.socialXxxFact: The original .xxx sponsored charter used voluntary self-identification by the adult-entertainment community and included goals around responsible practices and user choice. The 2024 renewal moved key commitments into Public Interest Commitments under the Base Registry Agreement.
en.socialXxxReading: A TLD can act like digital zoning. The social question is whether separation produces useful signaling and protection or simply relocates stigma into the namespace.
en.socialIslamQuestion: Who has the legitimacy to represent a global religious community in the DNS?
en.socialIslamFact: During the 2012 round, governments and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation challenged the .islam and .halal applications over community involvement, support and representational legitimacy. Neither string was delegated.
en.socialIslamReading: Some words are socially too large to behave like ordinary labels. The conflict was not only about technical competence but about who could credibly speak for a global community.
en.socialIdnQuestion: Who should have to transliterate their identity into someone else’s alphabet?
en.socialIdnFact: ICANN’s IDN framework supports domain names in local languages and scripts. Since 2009, the ccTLD Fast Track has enabled eligible countries and territories to request country-name TLDs in non-Latin scripts.
en.socialIdnReading: Internationalized TLDs turn script choice into an inclusion question: the global naming system becomes less dependent on Latin characters as the default doorway to the Internet.
en.guard6: Social significance is not inferred from registration volume. Registry charters, eligibility rules and documented community policies are FACT; the broader meaning assigned to them in this publication is a READING.
en.angle7: When does a TLD become a marker of language, locality, identity or belonging rather than simply an address?
en.release0716: The Social Life of the Dot: nine social cases, six social models, Explorer links and source-backed evidence on language, community, identity, safety and script inclusion.
en.release0717: Final audit hardening: corrected current ISO country codes in Explorer geography, aligned the publication snapshot to 4 October, clarified 2012 privacy handling and restored a self-checking release package.
en.release0718: Release integrity hardening: publication dates now derive from one state object; 2012 runtime enrichment no longer marks the full application corpus complete; archaeology counts are data-derived; 2026 round comparisons separate 1,663 submitted applications from 1,616 proceeding; historical private contention settlement is explicitly prohibited in 2026; release packaging, build metadata and QA are hardened.
en.heroPlain: In example.com, .com is the ending: a top-level domain, or TLD. Explore its history and check the data and sources here. .lugano is an application, not an operational extension.
en.release0719: Mobile journey hardening: the guided Internet walkthrough is now strictly viewport-bounded, puts the active explanation before its diagram on phones, reflows DNS and network diagrams on narrow screens, and keeps the current step in view when readers move forward or back.
en.release0720: Navigation clarity: the Italian menu now distinguishes “Stringhe contese” (competing applications for the same string) from “Controversie” (governance, legal or community disputes), removing an avoidable semantic ambiguity without changing the underlying sections or research data.
en.release0721: Automatic language entry: the root now respects an explicit saved language choice, otherwise detects the ordered browser language preferences, maps supported regional variants to EN / IT / DE / FR and falls back to English when no supported preference is available. Direct language URLs remain authoritative.
en.release0722: Guided-address focus: the sample URL now moves its visual emphasis with the walkthrough: the readable host name, the normally invisible DNS root dot, the TLD, the resolved IP, the network path, the HTTPS scheme and the requested page. The root dot appears only while it is being explained.
en.journeyTldAnswer: Points to the DNS for example.com
en.journeyAddressLane: An URL gives the browser three instructions
en.journeyUrlHowBody: Use the Web over a protected connection
en.journeyUrlWhereBody: Find this name and the server behind it
en.journeyNowLabel: What the Internet is doing now
en.journeyNow0To: the browser separates the URL into parts
en.journeyNow0Hint: How to communicate · which name to find · which resource to request.
en.journeyNow1Hint: The browser asks a DNS resolver where that name can be reached.
en.journeyNow2Hint: The DNS hierarchy moves from the root to the TLD and then to the authoritative DNS.
en.journeyNow3Hint: The resolver gives the device the address returned by the authoritative DNS.
en.journeyNow4Hint: Routers and networks forward packets toward the destination.
en.journeyNow5Hint: TLS authenticates the server for that name and protects data in transit.
en.journeyNow6Hint: The server responds; the browser interprets the files and builds what you see.
en.journey0Key: A URL is not just a website name: it contains different instructions for the browser.
en.journey1Key: Names are for people; IP addresses let networks reach destinations.
en.journey2Key: .com is not decoration: it is a real level in the DNS hierarchy.
en.journey3Key: DNS does not carry the page: it turns a name into information that helps locate the service.
en.journey4Key: The IP identifies the destination; routers decide hop by hop how to reach it.
en.journey5Key: HTTPS protects the transport and authenticates the server for that name; it does not guarantee that the content is true or trustworthy.
en.journey6Key: The page is the response to a request: the domain is the name used to reach the service, not the page itself.
en.journeyRecapTitle: From the URL to the page, at a glance
en.journeyRecapBody: These are conceptual stages, not a stopwatch: caches and existing connections can skip or overlap some of them. The chain is what matters.
en.release0723: Teaching-first Internet walkthrough: the seven steps now follow one coherent story from URL to name, DNS hierarchy, IP, networks, HTTPS and page. The DNS root is explained inside the hierarchy instead of as an isolated step; a live “what is happening now” strip, one key takeaway per step, sequential DNS delegation diagram and final recap make the relationship between URL anatomy, name resolution and web delivery explicit.
en.release0724: Navigation hardening: every user-initiated section change now lands at the start of the selected section on desktop and mobile; the brand is a real home link and reliably returns to the top of the overview. Internal anchored links, dynamically rendered Explorer cross-links, section indexes and the publication stamp share the same offset-aware navigation behavior.
en.release0725: Pre-Reveal freeze hardening: browser-time external research enrichment is disabled so every visitor sees the same frozen corpus, and release/data-pack ZIPs are now written deterministically for repeatable SHA-256 hashes. Research data and the 4 October IANA snapshot are unchanged.
en.applicationCorpusFrozen: Reveal Day snapshot: the complete historical local rounds ({rounds}) remain frozen and reproducible, while verified 2026 records are added explicitly. Full local APS coverage is not yet claimed.
en.release0726: Home-only Internet walkthrough: the guided seven-step journey now belongs structurally to Overview, disappears from every other section, resets when the reader leaves and returns home, and preserves direct anchored walkthrough links. The How it works section now starts directly with the deeper domain and DNS material. Research data are unchanged.
en.release0727: Explorer filter repair: filters now use explicit compact labels, the IANA test type is localized instead of appearing as a raw “test” value, and a universal editorial macro-theme index covers every Explorer record. Theme filtering therefore works across the whole database while remaining clearly separate from official ICANN/IANA fields.
en.release0728: Navigation offset fix: primary section changes now account for both the sticky top bar and the sticky desktop section navigation, so the first content panel is never hidden beneath the menu. Mobile navigation and anchored in-section links keep their existing offset-aware behavior.

en.refusalsSubtitle: Why some applied-for strings never entered the DNS root
en.refusalsIntro: This is not a catalogue of 'rejections'. It traces source-backed reasons why selected applications did not reach the DNS root: administrative returns, eligibility failures, non-selection, public-policy decisions, technical-safety blocks and voluntary withdrawals.
en.refusalsBoundaryBody: Contention is competition for the same string. Controversies are conflicts over rights, legitimacy, public interest or control. Application outcomes explain why an application did not reach the root. A case can have more than one dimension, but the editorial story appears once, where its main causal mechanism belongs; the other dimensions remain structured data and cross-links.
en.refusalTaxonomyTitle: Six different ways an application can stop
en.refusalTaxonomySub: 'Rejected' is too crude. The process contains different gates, and withdrawal is not a rejection.
en.refusalTaxAdminBody: The application can fail before substantive evaluation: missing fee, incomplete submission or another formal defect.
en.refusalTaxSupportBody: An applicant seeking financial assistance can be excluded if it does not meet the support-program criteria.
en.refusalTaxEvaluationBody: Financial, operational, geographic or other criteria can prevent an application from advancing, sometimes after Extended Evaluation.
en.refusalTaxPolicyBody: Consensus GAC advice can create a strong presumption that an application should not be approved, subject to Board consideration.
en.refusalTaxTechnicalBody: A string can be stopped because delegation itself is considered unsafe, regardless of who applied for it.
en.refusalTaxWithdrawalBody: The applicant can leave voluntarily. That is an outcome, but it must not be mislabeled as an ICANN rejection.
en.refusalSnapshotTitle: What the 2012 funnel looked like in August 2013
en.refusalSnapshotSub: A snapshot at the end of Initial Evaluation. These categories were not all final outcomes, but they show why “not delegated” is not a useful synonym for “rejected”.
en.refusalCasesSub: Selected examples, not a complete catalogue of every non-delegation. Each isolates a different causal mechanism.
en.refusalDrawerSub: This string appears in a selected case explaining why an application did not reach the root. Outcome, contention and governance controversy remain separate dimensions.
en.refusalFeesQuestion: Can a TLD application die before anyone evaluates the idea?
en.refusalFeesFact: Yes. In the 2000 round, two of the 47 submitted applications were returned because the USD 50,000 application fee had not been paid. One covered .number / .tel / .phone; the other covered .wap.
en.refusalFeesReading: This is not a dispute and not a judgment on the string. It is the cleanest example of an administrative gate: no valid fee, no substantive review. The later delegation of .tel and .phone also shows that one failed application does not permanently condemn a label.
en.refusalFeesOutcome: The two 2000 applications were returned. .tel later entered the root through the 2004 sponsored round and .phone through the 2012 round; the original applications did not survive.
en.refusalNycQuestion: Is a withdrawal the same thing as being rejected?
en.refusalNycFact: No. ICANN recorded that the 2000 .nyc application was withdrawn because the applicant and ICANN could not agree on the treatment of confidentiality claims.
en.refusalNycReading: The stop came from the applicant-process relationship, not from a finding that .nyc was an unacceptable TLD. The same label later returned in the 2012 round.
en.refusalNycOutcome: The 2000 application disappeared from that round; .nyc was later delegated to the City of New York in 2014.
en.refusalGeoQuestion: Can a proposal be positively evaluated and still not be selected?
en.refusalGeoFact: In the 2000 proof-of-concept round, ICANN leadership later described .geo as having received a very positive staff evaluation, while the Board still declined to select it because potential DNS operational risks could not be fully assessed at that experimental stage.
en.refusalGeoReading: The 2000 round was a deliberately small proof of concept, not the later pass/fail pipeline. Non-selection could reflect portfolio design and caution rather than a defective application.
en.refusalGeoOutcome: .geo was not among the seven proof-of-concept TLDs selected in 2000. It remains outside the root.
en.refusalSupportQuestion: What happens when financial assistance is itself a gate to the application?
en.refusalSupportFact: Only three 2012 applicants requested financial assistance. .kids met the support criteria; .idn and .ummah did not. Under the support rules then in force, the latter two became ineligible for further review and their USD 47,000 fees were to be refunded.
en.refusalSupportReading: The striking point is that the stop did not arise from the semantic validity of .idn or .ummah. It arose from eligibility for a support mechanism that was coupled to continued participation in the round.
en.refusalSupportOutcome: .idn and .ummah did not continue. Ummah sought reconsideration; the request was denied, while ICANN directed that the concerns raised inform review of the support program.
en.refusalGccQuestion: Can public-policy advice stop an application before an objection case decides it?
en.refusalGccFact: The GAC issued consensus advice that the .gcc application should not proceed. The New gTLD Program Committee accepted that advice and directed that the application would not be approved.
en.refusalGccReading: The decisive event was the institutional public-policy gate. A separate legal-rights objection was terminated once the application could no longer proceed; later accountability challenges are secondary to the reason for the stop.
en.refusalGccOutcome: .gcc did not proceed in the 2012 round. The applicant’s reconsideration effort was unsuccessful.
en.refusalCollisionQuestion: What if the problem is the string itself rather than the applicant?
en.refusalCollisionFact: ICANN identified .corp, .home and .mail as exceptionally high-risk for name collisions with private naming systems. Delegation was deferred, and in 2018 the Board directed that the 2012 applications should not proceed, with full fee refunds available upon withdrawal.
en.refusalCollisionReading: This is the clearest technical refusal in the round: the applicant could change, but the collision risk attached to the label. It is therefore fundamentally different from a fight over who deserves the string.
en.refusalCollisionOutcome: None of the three strings was delegated from the 2012 round. ICANN later reaffirmed that prior applicants would receive no preferential right in a future round.
en.disputesBoundaryNote: A failed, returned or withdrawn application is not automatically a governance dispute. Its application outcome is modeled separately from controversy and contention.
en.release0731: Separates formal application stops from governance disputes, adds six sourced stop stories and an Explorer preset, and trims the browser-upload package to 99 files.
en.release0732: Reframes the former rejection/stop layer as Application outcomes, keeps contention and controversy independent, and adds source-backed outcome_reason fields to the historical application corpus without inferring undocumented results.

en.release0743: Explorer 2026 hotfix: replaces the impossible one-shot 980-row request with validated pagination across the public string API, caches the completed inventory locally, and fixes the 2026 and contention presets so cross-round strings remain visible.
en.contention2026Derived: Derived from the public 2026 application data. ICANN’s official high-level statistics do not yet publish a unique-string total; replacement choices and later similarity procedures can still change the picture.
en.contentionResolution2026Body: The 2012 round allowed private settlements and private auctions. The 2026 round does not: once contention sets are finalized, the permitted paths are Community Priority Evaluation for eligible Community Applications and ICANN’s New gTLD Auction. Private auctions, joint ventures and other private contention-resolution arrangements are prohibited.
en.strange2026Sub: AI agents, corporate identity, trust words and deliberately weird language now sit beside the historical oddities. These are applications, not delegated TLDs.
en.strangeHistoricalSub: The earlier cases stay here as fossils of previous Internet imaginaries. Their value is stronger now that the 2026 layer can be compared against them.
en.outcomes2026StatusBody: Reveal Day opened the pre-evaluation phase. The Replacement Period runs through 21 October, String Confirmation Day is 17 November, and the Community Input and Objections Period begins only then. The cases below are historical outcomes from earlier rounds, not 2026 results.
en.disputes2026StatusTitle: 2026 status: applications are public, formal objections are not open yet
en.disputes2026StatusBody: The Community Input and Objections Period begins on 17 November 2026 and is scheduled to run through 16 March 2027. The disputes below are therefore precedents that explain the mechanisms, not disputes already decided in the 2026 round.
en.economics2026Body: The standard evaluation fee is USD 227,000 per application before Applicant Support discounts and any conditional fees. ICANN reports 1,615 Reveal Day applications and 333 .Brand applications. These are application-market facts, not registry revenue and not a forecast of how many strings will reach the root.
en.social2026Title: 2026: social purpose is not the same as an ICANN Community designation
en.social2026Body: ICANN reports 16 Community-based applications. Other applicants can still pursue an explicit social mission without using that formal designation. .meow is a useful example: its nonprofit applicant says it intends to channel surplus registry revenue into queer community projects. That mission should not be confused with ICANN’s application-type label.
en.release0744: Post-Reveal editorial rebuild: updates contention, Strange Internet, economics, social framing, application outcomes and disputes around the 7 October 2026 data; replaces pre-Reveal future tense with current state; and makes official, derived and editorial claims visibly distinct.
en.sAgent2026: The current 2026 public application view shows 13 live applications for .agent, the largest identical-string cluster in the derived ranking.
en.iAgent2026: In 2012 the most sought-after label was .app. In 2026 it is .agent: a compact signal that the technological imagination has moved from mobile software toward autonomous agents.
en.sAgi2026: The current public data show 7 live applications for .agi.
en.iAgi2026: A specialist AI acronym has become valuable enough to trigger a seven-way contest for root-level naming space.
en.sOfficial2026: The current public data show 8 live applications for .official.
en.iOfficial2026: A word that suggests authority could become part of the naming infrastructure if delegated. Users might read trust into the label before opening the site; whether that trust is justified would depend on eligibility rules, verification and actual operation.
en.sChatgpt2026: OpenAI is among the 2026 applicants and .chatgpt appears among its revealed branded strings.
en.iChatgpt2026: The namespace is being treated as a product and identity layer, not merely a generic directory. The brand can move to the right of the dot.
en.sMeow2026: The nonprofit dotMeow Foundation says it applied for .meow and intends surplus registry revenue to support queer community projects.
en.iMeow2026: A deliberately playful string can carry a serious governance and funding model. It is also a reminder that social purpose must not be confused with ICANN’s formal Community application designation.
en.sItiswhatitis2026: .itiswhatitis appears among the 2026 revealed applications highlighted in post-Reveal coverage.
en.iItiswhatitis2026: The root can absorb not only industries and brands but entire pieces of Internet-native speech. The namespace is becoming a record of language as much as a map of institutions.
en.sFart2026: .fart was publicly disclosed as a 2026 application and became one of the round’s most conspicuous examples before Reveal Day.
en.iFart2026: The absurd is not a side effect of namespace expansion. It is evidence that applicants see cultural memorability itself as an asset worth an application fee.
en.sOpenai2026: .openai is among OpenAI’s revealed 2026 branded applications.
en.iOpenai2026: A company can now seek to make its own name part of the DNS hierarchy. That shifts the dot from a destination category toward controlled identity infrastructure.

Website updates cannot change either archived release.

en.insideEyebrow: A process observed as it unfolds
en.insideIntro: The 2026 New gTLD Program is not just a historical dataset. We can follow its decisive public events as they happen, with the .lugano application providing an unusually direct vantage point. This is a chronicle of milestones, not an application manual.
en.insideProgramBody: The official ICANN program defines milestones, conditions and possible outcomes. Its documents are the source for dates and procedural claims.
en.insideLandscapeBody: Reveal Day and later decisions show the global field: competing ideas, shared strings, objections, evaluations and changing expectations.
en.insideCaseBody: A real candidacy gives the research a participant's perspective, but only verifiable and publishable events enter this public record.
en.insideTimelineIntro: A concise, source-linked timeline. Entries distinguish documented events, the status at the editorial review date, announced milestones, uncertain timing and conditional outcomes. A future date is not a result.
en.insideOpenBody: The 2026 submission period begins. An infrequent policy cycle becomes a concrete opportunity for organizations to propose new top-level domains.
en.insideCloseBody: The submission window closes. From this point the proposed namespaces move toward public disclosure and evaluation; the final number and status are not inferred from the deadline alone.
en.insideRevealTitle: Reveal Day: the round becomes visible
en.insideRevealBody: ICANN publishes the applicants and applied-for strings. .lugano appears in the public application record, allowing the program-wide picture to be compared with a first-hand case.
en.insideReplaceBody: Eligible applicants may use a previously declared replacement string. The Reveal Day inventory is therefore a dated snapshot, not the final confirmed list. No replacement action is presumed for .lugano.
en.insideConfirmBody: ICANN is scheduled to publish the confirmed applied-for strings and revised contention sets. This remains an announced future milestone, not an event already completed.
en.insideReviewBody: String assessment, community input, objections and applicant/application evaluation unfold under the program's rules. The timing and outcome of individual applications cannot yet be asserted.
en.insideOutcomeDate: Date and outcome not yet known
en.insideOutcomeBody: Successful applications may proceed to contracting, onboarding and possible delegation. Other outcomes remain possible. This record will document public evidence, not promise an ending.
en.insideDisclosureTitle: A participant-observer, not an institutional account
en.insideDisclosureBody: The author is involved in the City of Lugano's .lugano application. Connecting the Dots remains an independent research publication, not an official City statement. Public records and clearly attributed observations are included; confidential application material and unverified assumptions are not.
en.insideMethodNote: This is a living editorial account. RR1 (9 October) and RR2 (11 October) are separate immutable Zenodo research snapshots; the present chronicle does not retrospectively change either.
en.insideMetaDescription: Follow the ICANN 2026 New gTLD round through verified milestones and public events, with .lugano as a first-hand case study and clearly marked future stages.
en.release0760: Adds Inside the Round: a public, four-language milestone chronicle of the 2026 ICANN program, with .lugano as a participant-observer case; preserves the frozen RR1 research release.
en.sectorEconomyTitle: What categories appeared in the earlier reconstruction?
en.sectorEconomyKicker: Historical comparison · classification by string or applicant
en.sectorEconomyIntro: The earlier 2012/2026 map grouped some records by applicant activity and others by the market suggested by the string. It supports an exploratory comparison of those categories within the classified subsets, not a measurement of growth or decline in the industries themselves.
en.sectorCoverage2012: 2012 applications classified in the historical map
en.sectorCoverage2026: 2026 records classified in the historical reconstruction
en.sectorDenominatorNote: The percentages use the classified subsets: 801 of 1,930 records in 2012 (41.5%) and 690 of 1,608 in the previous 2026 reconstruction (42.9%). The 2026 layer includes records reconstructed from per-string counts. Categories may describe the applicant or the string; these shares do not represent the whole round or a uniform industry census.
en.sectorChartTitle: Category shares in the historical map: 2012 and 2026
en.sectorChartSub: Percentages within each classified subset, using the earlier mixed classification of string themes and applicant sectors.
en.sectorChartAlt: Paired 2012 and 2026 bars compare category shares in the earlier mixed classification, including technology, finance, AI, crypto and digital trust. They do not measure the industries as a whole.
en.sectorMovementNewTitle: AI and crypto appear in the 2026 subset
en.sectorMovementNewBody: The 2026 subset contains records classified under AI and crypto; the equivalent editorial categories have no records in 2012. This describes the vocabulary and classification of these subsets. It does not mean those technologies did not exist in 2012, or establish future adoption.
en.sectorMovementFinanceBody: The finance category combines identified organisations with generic financial terms. Corporate or brand names and references to a financial market express different naming strategies; their combined share does not count the financial institutions participating in the round.
en.sectorMovementMediaTitle: Media and communications: a smaller share of the subset
en.sectorMovementMediaBody: In the historical classification, media and communications account for 13.7% of the 2012 subset and 8.0% of the 2026 subset. The category has a smaller relative share; this does not establish a decline in those industries or in their economic value.
en.sectorMovementTrustTitle: Identity and digital trust: a larger share of the subset
en.sectorMovementTrustBody: The cybersecurity, identity and trust category accounts for 0.9% of the 2012 classified subset and 5.4% of the 2026 subset. That is a larger share in this map, not a measure of growth in the industry. Any future practical value of the names would depend on governance, services and actual use.
en.sectorFinanceExampleTitle: Financial names: brands and shared terms
en.sectorFinanceExampleBody: A bank's own TLD and a term such as .bank describe very different allocation models. A string's sector does not establish who may register, who governs it, or whether it will be delegated.
en.sectorMethodBody: Economic-sector labels are editorial and applied consistently to the preserved 2012 corpus and the frozen 2026 primary-string inventory. Ambiguous and cross-sector cases are excluded from the classified denominator. The comparison is descriptive and provisional, not an ICANN statistic.

en.portfolioIntro: A TLD round is not only a collection of individual ideas. Some applicants seek dozens or hundreds of strings, turning naming into a portfolio strategy. Compare the legal applicant, the unit counted and the provenance before drawing conclusions.
en.portfolio2012Body: Donuts filed 307 applications and Google 101 in 2012. The locally archived Reveal Day list of 13 June 2012 contains 76 records for Amazon EU S.à r.l. These figures describe applications, not delegated TLDs.
en.portfolio2026Top1: Link Freedom Group Ltd · live primary applications
en.portfolio2026Top3: Registry Services, LLC · live primary applications
en.portfolio2026Body: The public APS export acquired on 11 October 2026 yields 158 applications for Link Freedom Group Ltd, 139 for XYZ.COM LLC and 77 for Registry Services, LLC, out of 1,614 published base Application IDs. These are project calculations by legal applicant; replacement records do not add applications.
en.arubaPortfolioTitle: Aruba: why 39 and 20 can both be correct
en.arubaPortfolioBody: Aruba announced 39 applied-for strings including replacements; the frozen secondary index lists 20 live primary applications for Aruba PEC S.p.A. These are different units and scopes. Adding or comparing them as equivalent counts would be misleading.
en.portfolioQuestion: Who controls a name: the applicant, the corporate group or the eventual registry operator?
en.portfolioReading: Large application portfolios reveal a strategy, not a guaranteed market position. Applications can fail, enter contention, be withdrawn or remain undelegated. Concentration at application stage is not identical to concentration of functioning TLD registries.
en.portfolioCaveat: The 2012 and 2026 figures are not a directly comparable corporate-group ranking. The 2026 counts use 1,614 published applications, including six existing-TLD variant applications; the official reported total is 1,615. They describe the captured applications and their original primary labels, not final confirmed strings or awarded TLDs.
en.researchPubTitle: Research that stays citable as the site evolves
en.researchPubIntro: Connecting the Dots combines an evolving public atlas with dated, reproducible research releases. The live site may change; each archived research milestone keeps a distinct, stable identity.
en.researchDoiLabel: Persistent identifier · current Research Release RR2
en.researchReleaseBody: RR2 consolidates evidence from Reveal Day, 7 October 2026. The Zenodo deposit was created on 10 October at 22:04 UTC and has a bibliographic publication date of 11 October 2026; the evidence cutoff remains 10 October. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23288603. The complete individual APS dossiers are not locally archived.
en.researchNextBody: ICANN has scheduled String Confirmation Day for 17 November 2026. New evidence about confirmed strings, replacements and contention may justify Research Release RR3 after source review. No future result is assumed.
en.researchVersionRuleTitle: A website version is not a research release
en.researchVersionRuleBody: Technical versions (v0.x.y) may change navigation, accessibility, translations and current editorial analysis. RR1 and RR2 are separate, permanently archived research snapshots and must not be silently overwritten. A substantial new evidence milestone receives a new research release and DOI.
en.researchCitationText: Bregy, R. (2026). Connecting the Dots: A Living Research Atlas of Top-Level Domain Expansion (Research Release RR2, Post-Reveal Evidence Consolidation). Zenodo. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23288603.
en.researchDoiPending: Archived research release and verifiable DOI:
en.researchPaperBody: Current working paper: {paperVersion}, revised {paperDate}. This independently updated draft has not been peer reviewed. It sets out the research question, sources, methodology and limitations; the immutable RR1 and RR2 deposits remain separately citable.
en.researchArchiveBody: The research manifest, GitHub tags, frozen source data and CITATION.cff support independent reproduction. RR2 is the second version in RR1’s original Zenodo concept series. The current site also archives the public APS listing retrieved on 11 October 2026: 1,614 base application IDs and 1,169 replacement records. Full individual application dossiers are not included. The current analyses and the frozen RR1/RR2 releases remain separate.
en.luganoWhyTitle: Why would a city seek its own top-level domain?
en.luganoWhyIntro: The interesting question is not whether a city can place its name after a dot. It is what public value, safeguards and services could justify operating a distinct namespace. These are criteria for evaluation, not promises already fulfilled.
en.luganoWhyRecognitionBody: A .lugano address could signal a connection with the city, but the suffix alone would not certify its owner. Any trustworthy use would require clear eligibility, verification and anti-impersonation rules.
en.luganoWhyGovernanceBody: A civic namespace raises choices about reserved names, fair allocation, security, abuse handling and review of disputed decisions. These choices must be made transparent if the application succeeds; a domain extension does not settle them automatically.
en.luganoWhyNameTitle: An address, not an identity certificate
en.luganoWhyNameBody: The DNS translates names into technical destinations. It does not, by itself, prove that a service is official or trustworthy. Verification, accessible public registers and clear responsibility could add that layer.
en.luganoWhyProgressiveBody: A possible sequence starts with a secure registry and transparent registration policy, then adds verified services and interoperable public-interest components. None of these stages is operational merely because the application is public.
en.luganoSwissTitle: What Swiss precedents can and cannot tell us
en.luganoSwissIntro: Geographic and place-linked TLDs already exist. They help frame questions about eligibility, operation and public identity, but they do not predetermine the governance or the outcome of the .lugano application.
en.luganoCityPeersTitle: Cities and territories have taken different paths
en.luganoCityPeersBody: Cases such as .berlin, .nyc and .zuerich show that geographic names can enter the DNS under different operators and registration policies. A shared geographic label does not mean a shared governance model.
en.luganoZurichBody: The existing .zuerich Registry Agreement is a useful primary source for examining a Swiss geographic TLD. It is a precedent, not evidence that .lugano has been delegated or would use identical rules.
en.luganoSwissFirstTitle: Distinctive value, not an invented first
en.luganoSwissFirstBody: Because .zuerich already exists, .lugano should not be presented as Switzerland's first geographic TLD. Its potential originality lies in the proposed public-interest use of naming, trust and digital commons, which would still need to be built and assessed.
en.luganoTwoPathsIntro: The City of Lugano documents its institutional project. Connecting the Dots studies the same round independently, with disclosed first-hand involvement and a broader historical lens. Neither should be mistaken for the other.

en.behindMetaTitle: Field Notes | ICANN 2026 investigations and open cases
en.behindMetaDescription: Source-backed observations on ICANN 2026: Reveal Day figures, the .wdo application and unresolved questions.
en.behindIntro: A timeline records milestones. Here we examine what public numbers and sources do not immediately explain: discrepancies, identities, rules and open questions. Each case separates verified facts from documented interpretation and unproven conjecture.
en.behindCaseTitle: One application missing. Two different questions.
en.behindCaseLead: The figures differed by just one, yet the distinction matters. A paid-application count, an official Reveal Day total and a frozen secondary index do not describe exactly the same publication state.
en.behindStatusPartial: Partly explained · one question remains open
en.behindCountOfficial: ICANN, 7 October · official Reveal Day applications
en.behindCountSecondary: Secondary snapshot of 7 October · observed on 8 October
en.behindCountSecondaryCaveat: The 1,614 figure comes from the frozen nTLDData-based index (480 applicants), not an ICANN-published application-level export.
en.behindExplorerBridge: The Explorer’s 2026 layer represents 1,608 applications associated with primary strings (980 distinct primary strings), plus six variant-only applications for existing TLDs. Its 1,614 indexed applications are therefore neither 1,614 new strings nor the complete set of 1,615 applications reported by ICANN.
en.behindExplainedTitle: The .wdo application: a documented absence from the public list
en.behindExplainedBody: ICANN's APS Applications page explicitly says that application WDO2627T-T45217 for .wdo (World Data Organization, China) is still undergoing an administrative check and is therefore absent from the public applications list. The application detail page independently confirms that status. This gives a documented explanation for why the visible list can contain one fewer application than the official aggregate. The independent secondary snapshot is consistent with that omission; its coverage is not being certified as a complete APS export.
en.behindOpenTitle: Why did the official count fall before Reveal Day?
en.behindOpenBody: On 22 September ICANN reported 1,616 paid applications proceeding. On 7 October the official Reveal Day total was 1,615. The verified public sources reviewed here do not identify which record accounts for the change or why. Withdrawal, administrative rejection, a payment issue or a timing adjustment would be speculation. This question remains open.
en.behindWhyTitle: Why should anyone care about a difference of one?
en.behindWhyBody: Because a statistic, an application record and a publishable application list are different objects. The exercise shows why researchers must capture the date, scope and source of a number before comparing it, and why public visibility should never be confused with acceptance, approval or eventual delegation.
en.behindMethodBody: The 1,616 and 1,615 totals are direct ICANN statements; 1,614 is a time-stamped secondary index preserved by this project. The APS footnote documents .wdo's omission, but does not explain the earlier change in ICANN totals. The two gaps are therefore tracked separately. This episode is a corrigible editorial observation, not a revision of the archived RR1 dataset.
en.behindUpdateTitle: What would close the remaining question?
en.behindUpdateBody: A dated ICANN explanation connecting the September and October totals, a change to the .wdo administrative-check record, or a public list that can be reconciled application by application. Any substantive correction will be dated, sourced and documented in the project history.
en.behindIndependenceBody: The author participates professionally in the City of Lugano's .lugano application, but this research is independent of the City's institutional communication. Only public evidence and attributable interpretations are included; no confidential application information is used.
en.behindSourcesPreface: Primary sources are labeled separately from the secondary index and project snapshot.
en.behindSourceList: ICANN APS · Applications list and footnote
en.release0765: Adds Behind the Round: a four-language, source-backed and independently indexable field-note series beginning with the two distinct Reveal Day count discrepancies, plus reviewable source provenance and open-question update triggers. RR1 remains immutable.
en.behindRevisionInitial: First publication: separated the two numerical discrepancies; verified the APS administrative-check footnote and explicitly left the earlier official-count change unresolved.
en.release0766: Search-metadata polish for the four Behind the Round articles: shorter descriptions and a proper Article image reference for Google rich-result eligibility. Editorial evidence remains unchanged.
en.release0767: Renames the ICANN 2026 submenus to Timeline and Field Notes in all four languages, with consistent page headings, SEO titles, research references and stable permalinks. Dataset RR1, the original evidence and DOI remain unchanged.
en.behindRegionalTitle: The regional discrepancy: a second check
en.behindRegionalLead: Only Asia-Pacific differs between the official Reveal Day application counts and the project's preserved secondary index. The applicant count also differs by one in precisely that region.
en.behindRegionalConclusion: Across five regions, official totals add to 1,615 applications from 481 applicants; the secondary index has 1,614 from 480. The .wdo applicant is in China. The regional match supports the APS footnote but does not replace a one-to-one reconciliation of all application IDs.
en.behindIndependentBody: On 8 October, Stéphane Bortzmeyer examined the public CSV: 2,783 total rows, 1,614 applications when replacement-string rows are removed, and 480 applicants. Exported rows, applications and requested strings are not interchangeable because one application can yield several rows. The independent check corroborates the visible shortfall but does not explain the earlier change in the official total.
en.behindCoverageTitle: A widely reported explanation is not a complete reconciliation
en.behindCoverageBody: CircleID placed the .wdo administrative check alongside the change from 1,616 to 1,615. In its 8 October notice JPNIC similarly described 1,616 paid applications, 1,615 published and one under administrative check. Yet APS already reports 1,615 active in its statistics while the independent public index identifies 1,614. These accounts are relevant interpretations, not an ID-by-ID reconciliation proving which application caused the earlier official decrease.
en.behindRevisionReconciled: Second revision: added a region-by-region check, independent CSV analysis and a distinction between CircleID's interpretation and what can actually be reconciled. The 1,616 → 1,615 change remains unresolved.
en.wdoCaseTitle: Two organizations, one acronym: who may seek .wdo?
en.wdoCaseLead: The .wdo applicant is the World Data Organization, launched in Beijing in 2026. But the World Design Organization dates back to 1957, uses WDO and holds a registered trademark. Is there already a legal dispute? Public evidence does not establish one.
en.wdoCaseStatus: Shared acronym documented · No verified dispute
en.wdoIdentityTitle: First distinction: they are not the same organization
en.wdoIdentityBody: ICANN names World Data Organization, located in China, as the applicant for .wdo under WDO2627T-T45217, still undergoing an administrative check. World Design Organization is a separate Montréal-based body involved in industrial design and using wdo.org. Sharing the initials WDO proves no corporate or institutional connection between them.
en.wdoOriginsTitle: Two histories, almost seventy years apart
en.wdoOriginsBody: World Data Organization was launched in Beijing on 30 March 2026; the Chinese Academy of Sciences reports that Tan Tieniu was elected council chair. World Design Organization was founded in 1957 as Icsid and adopted its current name in 2015. The application therefore concerns initials with an established public history, but that history alone cannot determine entitlement to the TLD.
en.wdoTrademarkTitle: A verifiable earlier right is not an automatic veto
en.wdoTrademarkBody: Canada's CIPO registry records the word mark WORLD DESIGN ORGANIZATION (WDO), filed on 23 October 2015 and registered as TMA1008130 on 2 November 2018, with active registration. Trademark protection has a defined scope: it does not automatically confer ownership of the .wdo top-level domain, nor prove that the organization has filed an objection.
en.wdoProcessTitle: What does the ICANN procedure allow?
en.wdoProcessBody: The 2026 Applicant Guidebook permits a Legal Rights Objection by a party with standing claiming infringement of existing rights, backed by evidence. ICANN announced a public-input and objections window running from 17 November 2026 to 16 March 2027. Possible standing is a starting point, not an adjudicated claim. As of 10 October, no objection from World Design Organization concerning .wdo has been verified.
en.wdoComplianceTitle: Compliance context, not an explanation for the check
en.wdoComplianceBody: Another documented fact concerns Tan Tieniu: the Chinese Academy of Sciences identifies him as a World Data Organization leader, while a 17 July 2026 US OFAC update lists him under Hong Kong Autonomy Act measures on the Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List. That entry concerns an individual, not proof that World Data Organization is itself designated. No ICANN source connects it to the administrative check of .wdo; a causal claim would be speculation.
en.wdoUnknownBody: ICANN has not published the reason for the administrative check on WDO2627T-T45217. There is no verified objection by World Design Organization, refusal, established infringement, or decision on the merits of the application. Neither the new organization's age, another body's trademark nor a leader's sanctions record can be used to infer the cause.
en.wdoFollowTitle: How this case will be followed
en.wdoFollowBody: A revision will require new primary evidence: an APS status change, published comments or objections involving .wdo, official statements by either WDO, a decision affecting the name, or a relevant OFAC change. Each change will be dated and sourced. Research must not invent a dispute before one exists.
en.wdoRevisionInitial: First publication: documented the two distinct WDO organizations, the Canadian trademark, ICANN procedures and OFAC's entry concerning a leader, without attributing any cause to the administrative check.
en.wdoMetaTitle: Two WDOs and the .wdo domain | Field Notes
en.wdoMetaDescription: Two organizations share WDO. ICANN, CAS and Canadian trademark evidence; possible rights, unproven objections and explicit research limits.
en.wdoSourcePreface: Primary institutional sources and registers. The overlap in names is documented; any consequences for the application remain unestablished.

en.field03Title: When the safeguards' own recruitment system failed
en.field03Lead: An email inbox refused outside messages, and ICANN says a submission portal closed 24 hours before its deadline. These are not rumours about gTLD applications: ICANN documented the two technical problems in the Independent Objector selection process.
en.field03Status: Documented procedural incidents · individual effects not quantified
en.field03Section1Title: An inbox that could not receive
en.field03Section1Body: On 30 June 2026 ICANN reported that the dedicated email inbox for Expressions of Interest from potential Independent Objectors had been configured to reject messages from external senders. The defect was discovered following a respondent's report. ICANN fixed the configuration but said the earlier messages could not be recovered.
en.field03Section2Body: ICANN reports that the EOI portal inadvertently closed on 30 May 2026, describing this as 24 hours before the deadline. The same notice identifies 1 June as the previously extended deadline. Without precise closing times and time zones, the calendar dates and stated 24-hour interval cannot be independently reconciled. Several parties were prevented from submitting; the technical cause remained unidentified in the 30 June report.
en.field03Section3Body: ICANN notified interested parties, offered an alternative submission channel and later kept the EOI open until all Independent Objector roles were filled. The public record does not establish how many emails were lost, whether anyone ultimately failed to participate or the cause of the early portal shutdown.
en.field03Section4Title: Why this is relevant to the 2026 round
en.field03Section4Body: Independent Objectors may raise Community or Limited Public Interest objections without representing a private applicant. Failures in their recruitment process therefore matter for procedural accessibility and trust. They do not prove a fault in TAMS, an altered Reveal Day application count, or misconduct in the evaluation of TLD applications.
en.field03SourceRole: ICANN · role and independence of the Objectors
en.field03Revision: Initial evidence review: ICANN incident notice, EOI extension and Objector mandate.
en.field04Title: 1,169 replacement strings: the extra rows behind Reveal Day
en.field04Lead: A CSV can have more rows than applications. Alternative strings, early deactivation labels and variant-only records explain several numbers that look contradictory when read without their definitions.
en.field04Status: Counted secondary records · individual deactivation reasons still require checking
en.field04MetricTotal: Replacement-string rows recorded in the secondary index
en.field04MetricActive: Replacement rows marked active in that index
en.field04MetricDeactivated: Replacement rows marked deactivated in that index
en.field04Section1Body: Stéphane Bortzmeyer's extraction counted 2,783 CSV records, but 1,614 application records after excluding replacement strings. The difference of 1,169 corresponds to the alternatives recorded by internet.Best. APS explicitly explains that a primary record and its replacement can appear separately while counting as one application in the official statistics. The official 1,615 figure remains a distinct source and is not silently replaced by 1,614.
en.field04Section2Title: 727 deactivated alternatives: what the label does not prove
en.field04Section2Body: In its Reveal Day reconstruction, internet.Best marks 442 replacement rows active and 727 deactivated. The figures describe alternative records, not 727 rejected main applications. ICANN defines 'Deactivated' as a final application-record status but says that non-selected replacement strings are deactivated after String Confirmation Day. The historical secondary labels therefore need row-level and timestamp checks before we attribute reasons or dates to every record.
en.field04Section3Title: 980 primary strings and a secondary list of 986
en.field04Section3Body: The project's frozen nTLDData string inventory contains 980 distinct primary strings associated with 1,608 applications. Six additional secondary-index applications are variant-only applications for existing TLDs, outside that primary-string inventory. internet.Best reports 986 distinct strings under its own extraction. The numerical match 980 + 6 = 986 is suggestive but not, by itself, a verified one-to-one reconciliation of string identities; that requires checking individual application IDs.
en.field04Section4Body: ICANN reported 1,663 submitted applications after the 12 August deadline and 1,616 paid applications proceeding on 22 September. Thus 47 submissions are outside the later paid-and-proceeding total. This is a change in eligibility and accounting stage, not evidence of 47 formal rejections. It also does not answer why the published figure shifted again from 1,616 to 1,615 on Reveal Day.
en.field04Section5Body: The replacement window runs 8–21 October 2026, with string confirmation scheduled for 17 November. Eligible applicants may elect an alternative only once; they cannot reverse that choice. An alternative identical to another proposed primary or replacement string is ineligible, and the Guidebook restricts coordination among competing applicants. Final outcomes must not be inferred from Reveal Day status labels.
en.field04SourceAPS: ICANN APS · how primary and replacement rows are counted
en.field04SourceIndex: internet.Best · secondary application and replacement list

en.economics2026DeepBody: The 263 preliminary identical-string contention sets contain 891 applications. That is 55.2% of the secondary index's 1,614 applications, although the 263 contested strings are only 26.8% of the 980 primary strings in the frozen nTLDData inventory. In internet.Best's applicant ranking, the five largest portfolios account for 491 applications, 30.4% of its 1,614-record base. Contention is not an awarded TLD, and a filed application is not a revenue forecast.
en.socialMeow2026Body: The nonprofit dotMeow Foundation raised €121,896 in Kickstarter pledges from 1,838 backers for its proposed .meow registry, against a €80,000 goal. The sum is a crowdfunding campaign result, not an established operating budget, a delegated TLD or proof of ICANN approval. The project illustrates community financing of the naming layer without being automatically equivalent to ICANN's formal Community application category.
en.disputes2026CaseBody: The preliminary identical-string sets include .agent (13 applications), .official (8) and .anime (2). The two .anime applicants are Toei Animation, which filed as Community, and Oinkadot. That contrast raises questions about cultural representation and business operation, but neither an objection outcome nor a winner has been determined. A name such as .official also raises trust questions; the string itself grants no public authority and is not evidence of deceptive intent.
en.howBit2026Body: The frozen 2026 secondary index shows 11 ICANN applications for .bit. Namecoin already uses .bit in a separate blockchain-based naming system. It is not a delegated TLD in the ICANN global DNS root and ordinary DNS resolvers do not automatically use Namecoin's records. This is a namespace collision risk to explain, not a claim that Namecoin is one of the 11 applicants.
en.researchPriorBody: RR1 · Reveal Day 2026 was published on 9 October 2026 and remains independently citable under 10.5281/zenodo.23262623. RR1 and RR2 belong to the same version series, with concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23262622. Cite the exact version used, not the latest one indiscriminately.

en.cyclesTitle: Economic cycles: what applied-for strings reveal (and what they do not)
en.cyclesLead: The dot-com bubble, platform expansion, crypto boom-and-bust cycles and current AI investment frenzy frame successive moments of demand for names. They are different waves, not one inevitable path from a popular term to a profitable registry.
en.cyclesDotcomTitle: The dot-com bubble: the web before the new rounds
en.cyclesDotcomBody: The speculative surge and crash around 2000 occurred before the 2012 mass gTLD application round. Its legacy is a useful warning: a boom in companies, websites or domain prices does not prove that a new top-level registry will succeed.
en.cyclesCryptoTitle: Crypto: more than one market winter
en.cyclesCryptoBody: Between the 2012 and 2026 rounds, crypto experienced repeated booms and contractions. A 2026 string application may signal renewed interest, but does not measure blockchain adoption, registry demand or an applicant's financial resilience.
en.cyclesAiTitle: AI: a different point in the cycle
en.cyclesAiBody: Generative AI is still undergoing rapid commercialization. The editorial 2026 inventory includes AI-labelled applications, while the 2012 editorial comparison shows none in that category. Different taxonomies and the long gap require caution: names are not economic forecasts.
en.cyclesPlatformsTitle: E-commerce, social networks and the physical economy
en.cyclesPlatformsBody: Platforms can create demand for recognisable identities without needing a TLD of their own. Conversely, banking, manufacturing, logistics, retail and public institutions may seek branded or sector-restricted namespaces as infrastructure rather than as speculative real estate.
en.cyclesCaveat: Method: this is a historical interpretation of sectors and digital-market cycles, not proof of causation. Do not equate an application with delegation, actual registry operation, second-level registrations or financial success.
en.cemeteryChapterCardDesc: Ended delegations, registry changes and projects never entering the root, with their distinct outcomes kept clear.
en.cemeteryEconomicsTeaser: The economic costs of running a registry also illuminate exits and failed projects. For evidence, chronology and distinct outcomes, continue to the dedicated chapter.
en.cemeteryLead: A signed registry agreement is not immortality. Some strings never reach delegation; others are delegated and subsequently revoked. Termination of an agreement may also lead to transfer to a successor instead of disappearance from the root.
en.cemeteryDoosan: Doosan notified ICANN in September 2015 that it intended to terminate the .doosan registry agreement; ICANN issued a termination notice on 1 March 2016. A corporate TLD can be abandoned even after obtaining its own namespace.
en.cemeteryLupin: ICANN's termination register records the operator-initiated .lupin termination and revocation of its delegation on 10 December 2020. This is a documented post-delegation exit, not merely an unsuccessful application.
en.cemeteryWed: ICANN terminated the .wed registry agreement in October 2020; the subsequent determination was to transition its operation. Termination of an operator and death of a string must therefore not be conflated.
en.cemeteryTaxonomy: Withdrawn or rejected application; signed contract without delegation; delegated TLD later revoked; registry operator replaced while the TLD persists. These categories must not be merged into a single mortality count.
en.cemeteryCaveat: These are documented examples, not an exhaustive mortality census. A reproducible global graveyard requires reconciling ICANN registry agreement histories, termination determinations and dated IANA root records before publishing any total.

en.helsinkiBridgeTitle: .helsinki: a city can also give up its TLD
en.helsinkiBridgeBody: In 2026 Helsinki initiated the voluntary termination of its registry agreement. This is a concrete counterpoint for anyone considering a city TLD: securing a delegation and sustaining it over time are different decisions.
en.helsinkiBridgeCta: Read the documented timeline and status
en.helsinkiCaseHistory: The City of Helsinki applied for .helsinki in the 2012 round. IANA records the TLD as registered on 10 December 2015 and documents delegation in a report dated 21 January 2016. The city's official registry website described the original goal of making municipal services easier to identify.
en.helsinkiCaseFact: On 28 May 2026, the City of Helsinki notified ICANN of its intention to terminate the registry agreement under section 4.4(b). On 19 August ICANN issued a preliminary determination not to transition the TLD to a successor. Public comment closed on 18 September.
en.helsinkiCaseStatus: Source status as of 13 October 2026: ICANN has not yet listed a final determination for .helsinki, and IANA still lists it as delegated. A termination notice does not itself mean that the TLD has been removed from the DNS root.
en.helsinkiCaseReading: Editorial reading: .helsinki illustrates that a city TLD can enter an exit process. That matters when considering the long-term cost, public value and stewardship of geographic identifiers. The cited sources do not establish the city's specific reasons for the decision.

en.econEditorialTitle2026: Words are a market. Not yet an outcome.
en.econEditorialIntro2026: In the 2026 round, competition for identical strings reveals applicants' economic expectations. Filing does not mean winning a TLD, and contention is not a direct measure of future demand.
en.econEditorialMarketBody: Our analysis of the 7 October APS snapshot finds 263 exact-primary-string groups comprising 891 applications. These are analytical groups, not ICANN's definitive contention sets. Replacements and subsequent evaluations can change the picture.
en.econEditorialPortfolioTitle: Intercap: applying as a portfolio strategy
en.econEditorialPortfolioBody: Domain Name Wire (7 October) attributes 71 applications to Intercap Registry: 58 for strings with identical-string rivals and 13 without such rivals in its analysis. These press figures require reconciliation with APS application IDs before being treated as official totals. This illustrates a portfolio strategy, not completed acquisitions.
en.econEditorialIdentityTitle: Brands, products and AI agent identities: different logics
en.econEditorialIdentityBody: ICANN reports 333 brand applications on Reveal Day. A corporate brand, a product name and a possible digital-agent identity are different strategies. Using TLDs as trust infrastructure for AI agents remains a hypothesis, not an established result.
en.econEditorialDisclaimer: Editorial analysis dated 14 October 2026. ICANN statistics, locally derived groups and third-party Intercap figures have different evidentiary status and must not be conflated.

en.iaStoryGroupConflictsLead: When applicants compete for a string or rights and interests collide.
en.iaStoryGroupLifecyclesLead: From applications never delegated to TLDs that ended or changed operators.
